Monday. When Baljeet Sir wrote 47 minus 19 on the board, Tejas's stomach twisted. The numbers seemed to slide around. He stared out of the window and stopped listening, though his notebook margins were full of beautiful drawn birds.
Wednesday. Baljeet Sir kept him back, not to scold. He put a tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten, on the desk. "Show me forty-seven." Tejas counted bundles slowly. Then he untied one to take nineteen away. "Twenty-eight," he whispered.
The next Monday. They did it again, and again, with the matchsticks and then with drawings of birds in groups of ten. When Tejas got a sum right on the board, nobody laughed, because Baljeet Sir had said on day one that nobody would. Tejas's hand shook a little less.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Sir put on the desk on Wednesday?
qa.a: A tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten.

qa.q: Why did Tejas stare out of the window on Monday?
qa.a: He was panicking and felt scared, so he shut off and stopped listening when the numbers seemed to slide around.

qa.q: Which approach helped Tejas make progress, and why?
qa.a: Hands-on matchstick bundles, patient repetition and a rule that nobody laughs let him see quantities and try without shame.

qa.q: How might Baljeet Sir see the drawings in Tejas's margins?
qa.a: He might see real talent and a way in, which is why he later used drawn birds in groups of ten.

grounding: Tejas panics in maths though good at art, and hands-on materials, patient repetition and no shaming let him progress.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting, Tanuja sat on the small plastic chair clutching Mahima's report card. Science: 42. English: 38.
In the corridor, another mother had just said, "Tuition every day, that's what she needs." Tanuja's face still burned.
"I don't know whether to push her harder or protect her," she told Mrs Kapoor, the class teacher. "She cries over spellings every night."
Mrs Kapoor opened a folder. "The special educator has noticed she mixes letters. We can give her extra time and oral tests. But look here." She showed a drawing from art class, a detailed map of their colony, every house labelled with pictures.
Tanuja laughed through wet eyes. "She draws all day."
"Then let's make sure she knows she's good at something," said Mrs Kapoor. They set a meeting with the educator for Monday.

qa.q: What mark did Mahima get in English?
How did Tanuja feel after the other mother's comment?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, her face still burning, and torn between pushing Mahima and protecting her.

qa.q: What steps helped Tanuja feel steadier?
qa.a: Working with the school's special educator on extra time and oral tests, and celebrating Mahima's talent for drawing to keep her confidence up.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima at home in the evenings?
qa.a: She seems frustrated and upset, crying over spellings every night, which is why protecting her confidence matters.

grounding: Tanuja, worried about grades and comments, is torn between pushing and protecting, and working with the school and celebrating her daughter's talent steadies her.

passage:
Parveen could stand on the grain-market steps in Raichur and tell a ghost story that made the whole lane go quiet. She saw every scene like a film in her head.
But in the half-yearly exam she finished only two of five answers. Her spellings wandered; she read each question three times. The paper came back red. "You know this," her friend Charu said. "You explained photosynthesis to me with drawings."
Parveen wanted to tear the paper. "Maybe I'm just slow."
Charu's mother, a nurse, told them the district hospital could assess her reading and writing. It took two visits and a long form. After that, the school approved extra time and a reader for the board exams.
In the prelims, Parveen finished every answer. Her marks jumped. "That's what I actually know," she said, staring.

qa.q: How many answers did Parveen finish in the half-yearly exam?
qa.a: Only two of five answers.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the paper came back red?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and discouraged, wanting to tear the paper and wondering if she was just slow.

qa.q: What turned things around for Parveen?
qa.a: An assessment at the district hospital led to permitted extra time and a reader, so her exam marks could show what she really knew.

qa.q: How does Charu see Parveen's ability?
qa.a: Charu believes in her, having seen her explain photosynthesis with drawings, and is sure the red marks do not show what Parveen knows.

grounding: Parveen thinks in pictures and tells stories brilliantly but struggles under time limits until an assessment and permitted accommodations show what she knows.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage:
Gurleen Ma'am had taught in the Nabha government school for twelve years, and something about Disha puzzled her. In class discussion Disha explained the causes of the monsoon better than anyone. Yet her written test was half blank, the letters cramped, some words spelled three ways.
In the next reading round, Gurleen noticed Disha's shoulders creep up as her turn came closer. Her eyes went flat and far away.
Gurleen skipped her without comment. After class she said quietly, "Your answer about the winds today was excellent. Writing seems much harder than speaking for you. Would you be okay if I talked to your mother about a screening at the block resource centre?"
Disha hesitated, then nodded.
From then on, Gurleen let her answer some questions aloud in tests and never asked her to read aloud without warning.

qa.q: What did Disha explain better than anyone in class discussion?
qa.a: The causes of the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Gurleen Ma'am feeling as she compared Disha's speaking and writing?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and concerned, sensing the gap came from a learning difference rather than laziness.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen Ma'am's steps would help other teachers?
qa.a: Praising the ideas, suggesting a screening, allowing oral answers and not making the student read aloud on the spot separate a learning difference from lack of effort.

qa.q: What is it like for Disha as her reading turn comes closer?
qa.a: She feels tense and anxious, her shoulders creeping up, and seems to go somewhere far away to cope.

grounding: Gurleen Ma'am notices the gap between Disha's strong oral answers and weak written work, suggests screening, avoids reading aloud on the spot and values her ideas.

passage:
In her first term at university in Aarhus, Xin sat in the library with an audiobook in one ear and her notes turning into text through a voice tool. It worked. But the exam form had a box: "Do you need adjustments?" She left it empty for a week.
"I don't want them to think I'm cheating," she told her flatmate. Her cheeks went pink just saying it.
Finally she knocked on her tutor Emil's door. "I read very slowly. Letters jump. I use audio and voice tools. Could I have extra time?"
Emil nodded. "Of course. Thanks for telling me. Send me the form today."
In the exam, with the extra half hour, Xin wrote the best essay of her year. When it came back with an A, she took a photo and sent it to her mother.

qa.q: Who did Xin tell about reading very slowly?
qa.a: Her tutor Emil.

qa.q: Why did Xin leave the adjustments box empty for a week?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and worried that people would think she was cheating, her cheeks going pink just saying it.

qa.q: What helped Xin show her real ability?
qa.a: Telling Emil honestly and getting extra time, along with her audio and voice tools, let her write her best essay.

qa.q: How does Emil see Xin's request?
qa.a: Emil sees it as a normal, reasonable request and is glad Xin spoke up.

grounding: Xin feels embarrassed to ask for extra time but shares her difference with her tutor, earns understanding and shows real ability, feeling proud.

passage:
Monday. In the mall washroom, the hand dryer roared. Amandeep, two, screamed and clawed at Papa's shirt. Mohit carried him straight out.
Thursday. At home, Mohit switched on the hair dryer on low, far away in the next room. Amandeep peeked, hands on his ears, then went back to his blocks.
The next Monday. In the washroom, Mohit said, "Loud noise coming. Hands on ears?" Amandeep covered his ears, looked, and did not scream.

qa.q: What did Mohit switch on at home on Thursday?
qa.a: The hair dryer, on low, far away in the next room.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the hand dryer roared?
qa.a: He felt frightened and overwhelmed, screaming and clawing at Papa's shirt.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: He calmly took Amandeep out, then let him meet the sound gently and warned him first, instead of forcing him to stay.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel on the next Monday when Amandeep does not scream?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and proud of his son's small step.

grounding: Toddler Amandeep screams at a hand dryer, and calm, gentle exposure helps his body cope better than force.

passage:
At his primary school in Kraków, Yosef was known as the boy who sulked. He kept pulling at the back of his jumper where the tag scratched. The strip lights buzzed in his eyes. At lunch he ate in the corridor because the canteen smell of cabbage made him gag. When the bell rang, he flinched and snapped at whoever was nearest.
His teacher, Mr Marek, noticed one day that Yosef's shoulders dropped when the lights were off for a film. After class he asked, "Which things bother you most?" Yosef listed them, surprised anyone wanted to know.
The next week Yosef had a seat by the window, far from the bell, and a pair of soft ear defenders in his desk. His mum cut out all the tags. By Friday he laughed in class for the first time that term.

qa.q: Where did Yosef eat lunch?
qa.a: He ate in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when he snapped at people after the bell?
qa.a: He felt jangled and irritable because the noise, lights and smells were genuinely uncomfortable for him.

qa.q: What small changes helped Yosef, and why?
qa.a: A window seat far from the bell, ear defenders and tag-free clothes reduced the discomfort, so he no longer needed to withdraw or snap.

qa.q: How does Mr Marek see Yosef after their talk?
qa.a: He sees that Yosef's sulking came from real discomfort, not a bad attitude, and wants to help.

grounding: Yosef can't bear tags, lights, the canteen smell and the bell and seems irritable and withdrawn, and a quiet seat and ear defenders help.

subtype: Family member misreading it as fussiness [Receiver]
passage:
The wedding car was leaving in fifteen minutes, and Jyoti, nine, was on the floor in her new sequinned lehenga, crying. "It's scratching! It's like ants!"
Baljeet Chacha stood in the doorway. "Such drama! Everyone else is wearing one. Just get up, beta."
Jyoti tugged at the waist until her skin was red.
Her mother knelt and looked at the red marks. "Chacha, look. It's really rubbing her." She thought fast. "Jyoti, wear your soft cotton slip underneath. We'll pin the waist looser."
It took seven minutes. Jyoti stood up, tried a twirl, and nodded.
In the car Chacha said, "Maybe I was wrong. My brother hated woollen socks as a boy. We all called him fussy." Jyoti leaned against her mother and breathed out.

qa.q: What did Jyoti wear underneath the lehenga?
qa.a: Her soft cotton slip.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when Chacha called it drama?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, not believed, while the itching was really hurting her skin.

qa.q: What did Jyoti's mother do that reduced the battle?
qa.a: She listened, looked at the red marks, believed Jyoti and tried a quick adjustment, a soft slip and a looser waist.

qa.q: What would change if Chacha had kept insisting Jyoti was being dramatic?
qa.a: Jyoti would have spent the wedding sore and miserable, and learned that adults don't believe her when something hurts.

grounding: Jyoti's uncle thinks she is being dramatic about an itchy outfit, and her mother's listening, belief and small adjustment end the battle.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10 science trip.
Yusuf chewed through two pencil caps on the bus and asked to play loud music on his headphones. At the museum he kept tapping the railings. When I gave him a squeeze ball, he calmed a lot and asked good questions about the rockets.
Nandini, in the same group, covered her ears in the crowded dome and wouldn't eat the canteen food. She seemed anxious, and her hands were shaking.
Afterwards I met them one by one. Yusuf now keeps a fidget and chewing gum in his bag for long days. Nandini made a card: step out when crowds get loud, bring her own lunch. Both said it helped to know their bodies weren't "being weird," just asking for different things.

qa.q: What did the counsellor give Yusuf at the museum?
qa.a: A squeeze ball.

qa.q: How did Yusuf seem to feel before he got the squeeze ball?
qa.a: He seemed restless and unsettled, chewing, tapping and wanting loud music, and was calmer once his body had something to do.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why was it useful?
qa.a: The counsellor met each student to plan: Yusuf keeps a fidget and gum, Nandini steps out of loud crowds and brings lunch, so both can manage their needs with self-knowledge.

qa.q: How might the trip have felt for Nandini?
qa.a: The crowded dome probably felt overwhelming and scary for her, with covered ears and shaking hands.

grounding: A counsellor notes one teenager seeking input by chewing and fidgeting and another avoiding crowds and foods, and helps both plan with self-knowledge.

passage:
Thanks, Uma. So, I'm Karthik, and for years I thought I was just fussy. College lectures gave me headaches, the canteen made me want to run, and I blamed myself.
In second year I started a notes page on my phone. Every time I felt that jittery, trapped feeling, I wrote down where I was. After a month the pattern was obvious: flickering tube lights, scratchy collars, clattering plates.
So I changed small things. I sit near the window now, away from the lights. I wear soft cotton shirts. I eat lunch at eleven-thirty before the rush. In group work I say one line: "Noise hits me hard, so I'll take the quiet corner." People just say okay.
The headaches mostly stopped. Honestly, looking after myself like that isn't fussy. It's how I get to actually be there.

qa.q: What time does Karthik eat lunch now?
qa.a: At eleven-thirty, before the rush.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel before noticing the pattern?
qa.a: Karthik felt jittery and trapped in certain places and put it all down to being fussy.

qa.q: What steps from Karthik's story could help someone with similar triggers?
qa.a: Track where discomfort happens, choose seating, clothes and routines to ease it, and explain the need to others in one short line.

qa.q: How might classmates in Karthik's group see the one-line request?
qa.a: They probably see it as simple and reasonable, which is why they just say okay.

grounding: Karthik learns personal triggers, chooses seating, clothing and routines to ease them, and explains needs briefly, treating accommodation as self-care.
